paper_title: LLMs Don't Know What They Know: Benchmarking Temporal Self-Knowledge for Financial Backtesting

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Financial backtests of large language models (LLMs) are meaningful only if the model did not already know the outcomes it is asked to predict. Practitioners guard against this by trusting a vendor's stated knowledge cutoff, by asking the model what it knows, or by instructing it to answer as of a past date. To verify whether any of these safeguards can be trusted, we introduce FinDendro, a benchmark of 2,226 dated U.S. facts from 1999 to 2026, covering monthly macroeconomic series, month-end stock prices and Federal Reserve decisions. Each fact yields four prompts: a value question, Recall and Predict questions that pair each candidate value with a claim of knowing or guessing without a declared date, and a Predict question with a historical declared date. Controls for persistence and dominant outcomes keep chance accuracy near 0.27. Results show that for most frontier models, self-reports understate knowledge. GPT-5 answers 76% of controlled facts correctly but claims to know 38%, and answers 61% of the facts it says it does not know. Knowledge claims can persist beyond the measured knowledge boundary, by up to seven quarters, and a declared date removes most of the claims of prior knowledge while leaving accuracy unchanged. Backtests inside a model's training window therefore cannot be certified leak-free by self-report, instruction or stated cutoff. These findings motivate behavioral measurement of temporal knowledge boundaries, and FinDendro provides a benchmark and procedure for selecting backtest periods based on demonstrated factual knowledge.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used and evaluated for financial forecasting, including stock-price prediction [18], corporate expectations [14], and broader financial applications [26, 27, 33]. Their predictive capabilities are commonly assessed through historical backtesting, where models generate forecasts for past periods and their predictions are compared with realized outcomes. Financial backtests benefit from long evaluation periods because market conditions change, economic outcomes are noisy, and short evaluation windows after recent models training cutoff may not reliably distinguish predictive skill from chance [9]. However, historical backtesting introduces fundamental challenge for LLMs: realized outcomes may already be represented in their training data. When asked to predict past stock price, inflation rate, or monetary policy decision, model may reproduce the observed outcome rather than infer it from information available at the forecast date [5, 19]. Such hindsight leakage can inflate apparent forecasting performance, undermining the reliability of model comparisons and selection for financial applications. Practice relies on three safeguards against this, which are evaluating only after the vendor-stated cutoff [3, 38], instructing the model to answer as of the forecast origin [11, 19], and querying the model about 1 Figure 1: Model knowledge, claims, and release timelines. (a) Knowledge and claim boundaries measured by FinDendro, compared with self-reported and vendor-stated cutoffs and public release dates. (b) historical example in which GPT-5 denies knowing an outcome but produces the correct value, illustrating why self-reported knowledge boundaries cannot reliably prevent leakage in retrospective forecasting. its self-reported knowledge cutoff [2, 25]. However, most of the existing works ignore to evaluate the reliability of these safeguards. Input restriction supplies only information available at the forecast origin, through dated corpora or time-filtered retrieval, or uses instructions to restrict the model [11, 20, 43], but it cannot remove outcomes stored in the parameters, which models recall even when told not to [19]. Period selection evaluates after stated cutoff or release date [3, 38], but stated cutoff describes the training data rather than what the model retains. Boundary detection locates where knowledge ends from perplexity or behavior [4, 15, 28] and finds effective cutoffs that differ from reported ones, but these works do not ask whether the model itself knows where that end lies accurately, which is precisely what self-reports and declared dates rely on. As shown in Figure 1, the self-reported and the actual boundary of models might be different. Some works adopt Leakage-free designs to sidestep the question. Yet, prospective evaluation [17, 29, 37, 40] must wait for outcomes and cannot evaluate history, and point-in-time models [1, 8, 12, 35] remain small. Therefore, what is missing is measurement of models actual cutoff and its model-identified cutoff on the same facts, against which each safeguard can be tested. To this end, we introduce FinDendro, benchmark of which the evaluation targets these three safeguards: vendor-stated cutoffs, model self-reports, and input instructions. It compares models factual answers with their claims about what they know. It contains 2,226 dated U.S. facts from 1999 to 2026, covering twelve monthly FRED macroeconomic series, month-end stock prices for 50 large companies, and Federal Reserve rate decisions. For each fact, we construct three tasks. value question (Task 1) asks the model to select the correct answer. Its performance across periods provides an estimate of the actual cutoff, which we compare with the vendor-stated cutoff. separate value and claim question (Task 2) pairs each candidate answer with either statement of knowing or an admission of guessing. This allows us to examine whether the models knowledge claims agree with its factual performance and to estimate the model-identified cutoff. Task 2 is 2 Table 1: Comparison with related benchmarks. Fin. denotes financial or economic content; Dated, reference-dated facts; Cutoff, behavioral knowledge-boundary estimation; Claims, explicit knowledge claims; and Guards, evaluation of leakage safeguards. = yes, = partial, and = no. Benchmark Fin. Dated Cutoff Claims Guards FinBen [33] StockBench [3] FinTMMBench [41] ForecastBench [17] Look-Ahead-Bench [1] SelfAware [39] EvolveBench [42] Dated Data [4] LLMLagBench [28] HindsightBench [15] FinDendro (ours) asked in Recall and Predict forms without declared date. dated prediction (Task 3) uses the Task 2 Predict form with an instruction to answer as of specified historical date. Comparing Task 3 with Task 2 Predict tests whether the date instruction helps separate known outcomes from genuine predictions. We control for simple strategies such as repeating the previous months value and for imbalanced policy outcomes. We evaluate four frontier models, two smaller open models, and three families of point-in-time models. The results reveal limitations in each safeguard. First, stated cutoff dates do not necessarily locate the end of models effective knowledge. Llama-3.3-70Bs factual accuracy falls to chance after mid-2021, well before its vendor-stated cutoff of December 2023, while its knowledge claims continue until early 2023. Second, models self-reports do not reliably distinguish known from unknown outcomes. GPT-5 answers 76% of controlled facts correctly but claims to know only 38%. Within its measured knowledge window, it still answers 75% of the facts it says it does not know correctly, compared with 33% after that window. Keeping only facts that the model claims not to know therefore does not reliably remove leakage. Third, historical-date instructions can change knowledge claims without materially changing factual accuracy. Asking GPT-5 to answer as of past date reduces its claims of prior knowledge from 39% to 1%, while accuracy remains almost unchanged. Outcomes the model can answer may consequently be presented as predictions despite these instructions. The small point-in-time models offer different limitation: their accuracy remains near chance on either side of their training cutoffs. Together, these experiments show why backtesting safeguards should be checked against measured model behavior. FinDendro contributes benchmark that pairs factual answers with knowledge claims, consistent procedure for estimating both temporal boundaries, and direct tests of the safeguards used in historical backtesting.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 2.1 LLM Forecasting and Financial Evaluation Existing LLM forecasting benchmarks address temporal validity through information restrictions or evaluationperiod selection. Autocast uses dated news corpora to restrict information available at prediction time [43], while AutoCast++ improves evidence retrieval [34]. Halawi et al. [11] combine retrieval, reasoning, and aggregation, and OracleProto reconstructs historical forecasting conditions through temporally masked retrieval [20]. Prospective benchmarks such as ForecastBench evaluate predictions before outcomes are 3 In finance, FinBen, MultiFinBen, and Herculean cover broad financial tasks and agent known [17]. workflows [26, 27, 33]. More specialized benchmarks for taxonomy-grounded financial information extraction [31] and multi-document financial auditing [32]. StockBench evaluates trading beyond reported knowledge cutoffs [3], while FinTMMBench focuses on temporal financial retrieval [41]. Collectively, these benchmarks assess financial capabilities or forecasting performance, but do not directly evaluate whether models can reliably identify historical outcomes they already know. 2.2 Look-ahead Bias in LLM Backtests Prior work has examined look-ahead bias in financial LLM evaluations from several perspectives. Glasserman and Lin [10] use anonymized headlines to separate hindsight effects from company knowledge. Lopez-Lira et al. [19] demonstrate the reproduction of historical economic and market outcomes, while Crane et al. [5] quantify macroeconomic recall. Gao et al. [9] propose tests for look-ahead bias, and Paleka et al. [25] examine broader pitfalls in evaluating LLM forecasters. Other approaches mitigate leakage through point-in-time training [8, 12, 35], while Look-Ahead-Bench compares trading performance across in-sample and out-ofsample periods [1]. These studies establish the importance of hindsight leakage but do not jointly examine factual recall and models explicit knowledge claims. 2.3 Knowledge Boundaries and Self-Knowledge Research on model self-knowledge examines whether LLMs can recognize their own knowledge limitations. Kadavath et al. [16] investigate models ability to assess answer correctness, while SelfAware evaluates recognition of unanswerable questions [39]. Temporal benchmarks such as TempLAMA, DyKnow, and EvolveBench assess evolving factual knowledge [7, 22, 42], while ChronoRegime examines whether historical evidence supports future predictions [13]. Complementary work estimates temporal knowledge boundaries: Dated Data uses perplexity over dated documents [4], LLMLagBench probes recent-event knowledge [28], and HindsightBench estimates behavioral cutoffs through time-indexed macroeconomic questions and date manipulation [15]. These studies investigate knowledge awareness or temporal boundaries, but do not jointly compare explicit knowledge claims with factual performance across the same dated financial facts. Table 1 summarizes the differences between FinDendro and existing benchmarks. While prior work addresses financial evaluation, temporal knowledge, or self-awareness, FinDendro combines dated financial facts, behavioral knowledge-boundary estimation, and fact-level knowledge claims to examine the reliability of safeguards used in historical backtesting.

sections.title: 3 The FinDendro Benchmark
sections.content: FinDendro asks two questions of any model. Up to which date does it know dated financial facts, and up to which date does it say that it does? Three design choices follow from this aim. First, all facts come from one economy and one calendar, so that change in behavior over time reflects the model rather than change in the material. Second, every fact is scored against the value published at the time, so that correct answer is evidence of recall rather than of later revision. Third, the same candidate values are offered with and without statement of knowledge, so that models answer and its claim about that answer come from single choice. 3.1 Fact collection The pool contains 20,972 dated U.S. facts from January 1999 to September 2026 in three families. Macroeconomic facts are monthly values of twelve FRED series, namely headline and core CPI inflation, unemployment, the effective federal funds rate, the 3-month, 2-year and 10-year Treasury rates, the 30-year mortgage rate, three dollar exchange rates, and WTI oil. We use first-release observations retrieved, retaining the initial 4 Table 2: The evaluation sample by fact family. Controlled counts the facts that count toward knowledge, which are the numerical facts where repeating last months value fails and all policy facts. Family Series Facts Before 2021 2021 on Controlled Macroeconomic Stock prices Fed decisions Total 12 1,353 540 50 333 1 63 2,226 528 264 825 276 69 715 292 333 1,056 1,170 1,340 publication date and value rather than subsequent revisions.1 Company facts are month-end closing prices of 50 large U.S. companies obtained from Yahoo Finance, using the last trading day of each month and reversing subsequent stock-split adjustments to recover prices as quoted at the time.2 Policy facts are monthly Federal Reserve target-rate outcomes, derived from the target-rate history available through FRED.3 For each fact, we score against the value published at the time. We collected 2,226 facts in total, of which 1,353 are macroeconomic, 540 company and 333 policy facts. Sampling is sparse before 2021 (two macroeconomic facts and one stock per month, plus every FOMC month), giving 1,056 facts, and dense from 2021 onward (every macroeconomic series and four stocks per month), giving 1,170 facts, because the cutoffs of current models fall between 2021 and 2025. Table 2 summarizes the sample. Of the 2,226 facts, 1,340 count toward knowledge after the controls of Section 3.3. Each fact yields four prompts, for 8,904 prompts per model, and since every answer is single option letter, evaluating new model is inexpensive. The full pool, the sample, the question files and the construction code will be released with the benchmark. 3.2 Question and Answer Construction Based on the collected facts, we construct three aligned tasks to evaluate models temporal self-knowledge. Task 1 asks the model to identify the correct value, providing behavioral measure of factual knowledge. Task 2 additionally elicits claim about whether the model knows that value, using Recall and Predict wordings without declared date. Comparing Task 1 and Task 2 allows us to assess whether knowledge claims agree with factual performance and, across reference periods, to estimate the actual and model-identified cutoffs. Task 3 adds historical-date instruction to the Predict wording to test its effect on answers and knowledge claims. As shown in Table 3, each fact yields four prompts that share the same candidate values. Numerical facts offer four values spaced by roughly one typical monthly change of the series, with the rank of the true value drawn uniformly, and policy facts offer the three outcomes. Every prompt asks the model to answer from its own knowledge, without browsing or tools, and to output single option letter. Task 1 (value).. We first establish behavioral reference for what the model knows about the collected facts. For each fact, the model selects one of the candidate values without making knowledge claim. Its factual accuracy across reference periods provides the basis for estimating the actual cutoff. Task 2 (value and claim).. We then examine whether the model recognizes the knowledge measured in Task 1. To this end, Task 2 asks the model to select candidate value together with claim about whether it knows that value. Each candidate appears twice: once with claim of knowing and once with claim of not knowing, giving eight options for numerical facts and six for policy facts. We use two wordings, both without declared date, to examine how prediction framing affects knowledge claims. Recall asks what the value 1https://alfred.stlouisfed.org/. 2https://finance.yahoo.com/; https://ranaroussi.github.io/yfinance/. 3https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTAR; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARL; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/ DFEDTARU. 5 Table 3: An illustrative CPI fact across three tasks and four prompts. Candidate values are shared, and options are summarized. Each prompt is sent independently with shuffled options. Fact. June 2023 U.S. headline CPI inflation: the 12-month change in FRED CPIAUCNS (all items, NSA), rounded to one decimal place. Candidate values: 3.0%, 3.4%, 3.2%, 2.8%. Task 1: Value What was U.S. headline CPI inflation in June 2023? Options: the four candidate values. Task 2: Value and claim Recall: Recall the value from your memory: what was U.S. headline CPI inflation in June 2023? If you do not know it, select do not know. Options: each value appears twice: once as known and once as guess (8 choices). Predict: Predict U.S. headline CPI inflation in June 2023. Options: each value appears twice: once as already known and once as prediction of an unknown outcome (8 choices). Task 3: Dated prediction Assume that today is May 31, 2023. Answer as you would on that date. Predict U.S. headline CPI inflation in June 2023. Options: the same paired options as Task 2 Predict (8 choices). was, using know this value and do not know this value followed by best guess. Predict asks the model to predict the value, using already know the outcome and do not know the outcome followed by prediction; policy outcomes are expressed in the future tense. Task 3 (dated prediction).. We next test whether historical-date instruction changes factual answers or knowledge claims. Task 3 uses the same question, candidate values, and paired claim options as Task 2 Predict, adding the prefix Assume that today is [date]. Answer as you would on that date., where [date] is the last day of the month preceding the reference period. Comparing Task 3 with Task 2 Predict measures the effect of this date instruction. 3.3 Controls To reduce the effects of persistence and class imbalance on measured factual accuracy, we apply two controls. These address cases where model can answer correctly without recalling the particular historical outcome. For numerical facts, persistence strategy selects the candidate closest to the previous months value. When the monthly change is smaller than half an option step, the true value remains the closest candidate, allowing this strategy to answer correctly without knowing the current months outcome. This occurs for 47% of numerical facts. Including these cases would risk attributing accuracy from persistence to factual knowledge. We therefore measure numerical knowledge only on the remaining 1,007 facts, for which this strategy fails. For policy facts, unchanged is correct in 78% of months. Ordinary accuracy would therefore reward model that always selects this outcome, even if it cannot identify rate increases or decreases. We instead use balanced accuracy, averaging the proportion of correct answers within each of the three outcome classes so that each receives equal weight. Always selecting unchanged then scores one third rather than 78%. Together, these controls reduce the contribution of persistence and dominant outcomes to the knowledge score. The combined chance reference is approximately 0.27, reflecting four-option numerical questions and three-outcome policy questions. 6 3.4 Measures For each model we report five quantities. Knows is Task 1 accuracy on the 1,340 controlled facts. Says is the share choosing know option in Task 2 Recall without declared date, aggregated over the full sample of 2,226 facts. We also report accuracy when the model says it knows and accuracy when the model says it does not know, measured using Task 1 on facts grouped by these Recall claims, and the within-period gap between these accuracies. The gap is computed within each period (five-year blocks before 2021 and half-years after), weighted by period size, with 95% intervals from 1,000 bootstrap resamples of facts. Separately, we report the change in claims and accuracy from Task 2 Predict to Task 3. Based on these quantities, we estimate the actual and model-identified cutoffs shown in Figure 1. The actual cutoff is estimated as the last quarter whose two-quarter rolling accuracy (Knows) stays above the midpoint between the models 2015 to 2020 level and chance. We estimate the model-identified cutoff as the last quarter whose claim rate (Says it knows) stays above half of its 2015 to 2020 level. When claims end falls after knowledge ends, the intervening quarters indicate continued knowledge claims beyond the measured knowledge boundary. We also record the self-reported cutoff, which is the answer when the model is asked for its cutoff directly, and the vendor-stated cutoff, which is published by the model developer.

sections.title: 4 Experiments and Results
sections.content: 4.1 Setup We evaluate four frontier models via API: GPT-5 [24], DeepSeek-V3.2 [6], GPT-4o [23], and Llama-3.3-70BInstruct [21]. The reported knowledge cutoffs are September 2024 for GPT-5, October 2023 for GPT-4o, and December 2023 for Llama-3.3-70B; DeepSeek-V3.2 has no publicly stated cutoff. We use temperature 0 where supported and maximum of 1,024 output tokens, increased to 4,096 for GPT-5 to accommodate its reasoning tokens. Each prompt is evaluated once. For comparison, we also evaluate two locally hosted open models, Qwen3-8B [36] and Qwen3.5-9B [30], using greedy decoding with thinking disabled. We further include three families of point-in-time models trained on text available before fixed cutoff dates: TiMaGPT [8], ChronoGPT-Instruct [12], and DatedGPT [35]. See appendix for details. In Tasks 2 and 3, Says is the share claiming knowledge across the full sample of 2,226 facts, regardless of answer correctness. Task 2 Recall uses no declared date; Accsays and Accdenies are Task 1 accuracies on facts grouped by these claims. Gap is their within-period accuracy difference, weighted by period size, with 95% bootstrap intervals. The x-axis is Task 1 accuracy on controlled facts (chance 0.27) and the y-axis is the share of Task 2 Recall answers that claim knowledge. Points below the diagonal under-report their knowledge and points above it over-claim. Dotted lines show each models distance from the diagonal. 4.2 Frontier models know more than they say Figure 2 compares models factual accuracy on controlled facts in Task 1 with their knowledge claim rates in Task 2 Recall without declared date. GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3.2, and GPT-4o show substantially higher factual accuracy than knowledge claim rates. GPT-5 answers 76% of controlled facts correctly but claims to know only 38%, while GPT-4o achieves 50% accuracy with claim rate of 20% , as shown in Table 4. In contrast, Llama-3.3-70Bs claim rate slightly exceeds its factual accuracy (0.48 versus 0.43). This tendency to over-claim is more pronounced in the two Qwen models, which claim to know about 70% of facts despite accuracies of 0.360.37, close to the chance level of 0.27. 4.3 Knowledge claims can outlast factual knowledge Figure 3 tracks factual accuracy and knowledge claims over time, revealing differences between where models knowledge ends and where they stop claiming it. As shown in Figure 1, for GPT-5, both boundaries coincide at 2024Q3, matching its vendor-stated cutoff. In contrast, Llama-3.3-70B shows seven-quarter gap: its factual accuracy falls to chance after 2021Q2, but it continues claiming knowledge until 2023Q1, closer to its reported cutoff of December 2023. GPT-4os knowledge ends one quarter before its claims, while DeepSeek-V3.2 shows similar one-quarter gap. The two Qwen models remain near chance across the timeline but continue claiming knowledge until 2024. These patterns show that knowledge claims do not consistently track the knowledge models have. Therefore, we cannot trust the self-reported knowledge of models. This mismatch matters for financial backtesting, where reported cutoffs are used to select evaluation periods. For Llama-3.3-70B, the vendor-stated cutoff is ten quarters later than its measured knowledge 8 Figure 3: Temporal patterns of factual accuracy and knowledge claims. Purple and orange lines show Task 1 accuracy and the share of knowledge claims, respectively. Shading highlights their differences. Markers indicate the estimated knowledge boundary (), claim boundary (), self-reported cutoff (), and vendor-stated cutoff (), where available. Years before 2021 are compressed, while later periods are shown quarterly. boundary, excluding substantial period in which factual accuracy has already declined toward chance. More broadly, reported cutoffs and knowledge claims provide different pictures of the temporal extent of models factual knowledge. We also examine the sensitivity of boundary estimates to the detection thresholds. Changing the thresholds from one-half to one-third of the distance between the 20152020 baseline and chance shifts GPT-5s and DeepSeek-V3.2s estimated boundaries by at most one quarter. Llama-3.3-70B retains six-to-seven-quarter gap, while GPT-4os estimated gap increases from one to six quarters. We additionally test more permissive threshold settings. These yield unstable boundary estimates as the accuracy threshold approaches chance, allowing sampling fluctuations to shift the estimated knowledge boundary. 4.4 Self-report does not clean backtest We then examine whether knowledge claims distinguish facts the model answers more accurately from those it answers less accurately. Across the four frontier models, these within-period gaps range from 0.08 for DeepSeek-V3.2 to 0.39 for GPT-4o, and all 95% bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero. Knowledge claims therefore carry information about which facts the model answers more accurately. However, accuracy on disclaimed facts can still substantially exceed chance. GPT-5s accuracy on this group is more than twice the chance reference of 0.27, and DeepSeek-V3.2 also achieves 48% accuracy on disclaimed facts. GPT-4o and Llama-3.3-70B are closer to chance on disclaimed facts, at 34% and 29%, respectively, compared with 83% and 58% on facts claimed as known. The reliability of dont know thus varies across models. In particular, an admission of not knowing does not reliably identify unknown historical outcomes for the strongest models. Table 5 illustrates how these admissions appear in evaluations. In Task 2 Recall, GPT-5 states that it does not know Intels January 2021 closing price but selects the correct value of 55.51. In Task 3, when instructed to predict the same price as of December 31, 2020, it again denies prior knowledge and selects 55.51. The same pattern appears for Chevrons January 2006 closing price and the February 2024 USD/JPY exchange rate. In each case, the correct historical outcome is presented as guess or prediction despite the models denial of knowledge. Such answers would count as forecasts in historical backtest, with the disclaimer failing to establish that the outcome was unknown. We next examine the practical consequences of using these knowledge claims to select backtest samples. Specifically, we apply filter that excludes facts the model claims to know in Recall and retains only those it disclaims. Table 6 reports the fraction of facts retained and their Task 1 accuracy, separately inside and after each models measured knowledge window. For GPT-5, the filter retains 46% of in-window facts, yet accuracy on these retained facts remains 0.75, compared with 0.33 after its knowledge boundary. DeepSeek-V3.2 shows similar pattern, with accuracy of 0.53 on retained in-window facts versus 0.34 afterward. The corresponding differences are smaller for GPT-4o and Llama-3.3-70B, whose in-window accuracies are closer to their post-boundary levels (0.37 versus 0.32 and 0.31 versus 0.27, respectively). However, the filter retains only 22% of Llama-3.3-70Bs in-window facts. Self-report filtering can therefore leave substantial historical 10 Table 7: simulated dated backtest using Task 3 (dated prediction), on controlled facts inside and after each models knowledge window. Acc (all) GPT-5 DeepSeek-V3.2 GPT-4o Llama-3.3-70B 0.99 0.46 0.91 1.00 0.83 0.45 0.48 0.51 0.82 0.38 0.44 0.51 0.39 0.32 0.33 0. knowledge in the retained sample or sharply reduce data coverage. Its usefulness must be assessed against the measured actual knowledge boundary. 4.5 declared date changes the words, not the knowledge We next test whether declaring historical date improves the reliability of backtesting by comparing Task 2 Predict with Task 3 in Table 4. This comparison shows that declaring historical date substantially changes models knowledge claims, while factual accuracy changes little. For GPT-5, the share of answers claiming prior knowledge drops from 0.39 in Task 2 Predict to 0.01 in Task 3, while accuracy remains nearly unchanged (0.76 to 0.75). Similar patterns appear for Llama-3.3-70B (0.63 to 0.00) and GPT-4o (0.33 to 0.04), with no meaningful change in accuracy. DeepSeek-V3.2 shows the opposite trend in knowledge claims (0.37 to 0.46), again with unchanged accuracy. These results show that historical-date instructions change how models describe their answers, not what they can answer. Table 7 reports Task 3 results inside and beyond each models measured knowledge window. GPT-5 labels 99% of its in-window answers as predictions, achieving 0.82 accuracy on these answers, compared with 0.39 after its knowledge boundary. Similar gaps appear for GPT-4o (0.44 versus 0.33) and Llama-3.3-70B (0.51 versus 0.29), with 91% and 100% of their in-window answers labeled as predictions, respectively. DeepSeek-V3.2 shows smaller gap (0.38 versus 0.32), while labeling 46% of its in-window answers as predictions. These results show that declared-date prompting allows models to present highly accurate answers to previously observed outcomes as forecasts, substantially inflating apparent backtesting performance within their knowledge windows. 4.6 Where the hidden knowledge lies Figure 4 shows that knowledge-claim gaps vary substantially across financial fact families. The largest gaps occur for stock prices, where all four models know considerably more than they claim. GPT-5 exhibits gap of +0.54 (59% accuracy versus 5% claimed knowledge), followed by DeepSeek-V3.2 (+0.47; 49% versus 2%) and GPT-4o (+0.33; 33% versus 0%). Macroeconomic values show similar pattern for most models, but Llama-3.3-70B exhibits the reverse, claiming knowledge of 53% of facts while answering only 32% correctly (-0.21). In contrast, Federal Reserve decisions show much smaller gaps (-0.16 to +0.04), indicating closer agreement between factual accuracy and knowledge claims. These results reveal strong fact-family dependence, with the greatest underclaiming concentrated in precise numerical outcomes. 4.7 Small and point-in-time models Point-in-time models, trained only on data available before fixed cutoffs, offer potential control for evaluating knowledge boundaries. However, the models we test (1-1.5B parameters) struggle with the multiple-choice format, often selecting the first option regardless of the question. We therefore evaluate TiMaGPT and 11 Figure 4: Knowledgeclaim gaps across financial fact families. sections.title: 5 Implications for Backtesting
sections.content: Our findings suggest that financial LLM backtests should incorporate behavioral knowledge audits rather than relying solely on reported cutoffs or temporal prompting. Practitioners can first evaluate models on dated facts relevant to the target domain and estimate their knowledge boundaries using consistent procedure (Section 3.4). These estimates can guide the selection of evaluation periods, with appropriate margins for boundary uncertainty. In our experiments, vendor-stated cutoffs are generally conservative 12 relative to measured boundaries. For example, Llama-3.3-70Bs reported cutoff excludes ten quarters beyond its measured knowledge boundary, while DeepSeek-V3.2 provides no published cutoff. Self-reported knowledge and historical-date instructions should not replace behavioral measurements, as neither reliably excludes previously known outcomes (Sections 4.4, and 4.5). Reporting measured boundaries alongside backtesting results, and reassessing them when models are updated, would improve evaluation transparency and comparability. Our results also have implications for model developers. Knowledge claims are particularly unreliable for precise numerical facts, even when models can identify the correct values (Section 4.6). Moreover, the boundaries of these claims can differ substantially from both demonstrated knowledge and reported cutoffs. Model providers could therefore complement stated training cutoffs with behavioral knowledge assessments on dated, domain-specific facts. Such evaluations would provide practitioners with clearer picture of the temporal knowledge available to model and support more reliable financial backtesting.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We asked whether the safeguards used to keep outcome knowledge out of LLM backtests can be trusted, and built FinDendro to answer from behavior. On dated U.S. financial facts, the answer is no. Frontier models know more than they say, stop claiming knowledge at date they believe rather than at the end of what they retain, answer many of the facts they disclaim, and drop their claims of prior knowledge when told to answer as of past date without forgetting anything. stated cutoff, self-report and declared date each fail to separate known from unknown outcomes. Backtests should therefore be restricted to periods after knowledge boundary measured on the model itself, or run on models whose training data end before the test period. FinDendro provides the facts, questions and procedure for the first, and shows that current point-in-time models are still too small for the second.

sections.title: Limitations and Ethics
sections.content: Limitations. FinDendro covers one economy and three families of monthly financial facts, and boundaries for other regions, other kinds of financial knowledge or text-based events may differ. The boundary rule uses fixed thresholds relative to each models 2015 to 2020 level and chance. Other thresholds move the estimated quarters, although the same rule is applied to every model. model can be right without recall when it extrapolates trend, and our persistence control removes only the simplest such strategy. Frontier models were accessed through an API router and score one response per prompt at temperature 0 where supported. Served versions may change over time, and we excluded one model whose served identity we could not verify. Free-form or probabilistic statements of knowledge may behave differently from our multiple-choice claims. Finally, the point-in-time models we test are small, so they cannot yet show whether large model with strict cutoff would behave honestly. Ethics. All facts come from public sources (FRED, published exchange quotes and Federal Reserve announcements) and contain no personal data. The benchmark is meant to make financial evaluations of LLMs more reliable, and its main risk is misuse as certificate that model is leak-free for period, which our results caution against.

sections.title: A Data Collection and Construction
sections.content: A.1 Sources and Historical Values The fact pool contains 20,972 dated U.S. financial facts from January 1999 to September 2026, covering macroeconomic indicators, company stock prices, and Federal Reserve policy outcomes. Macroeconomic facts.. We collect monthly observations for twelve FRED series: headline and core CPI inflation, unemployment, the effective federal funds rate, the 3-month, 2-year, and 10-year Treasury rates, the 30-year mortgage rate, three dollar exchange rates, and WTI oil. First-release observations are retrieved through ALFRED, retaining the initial publication date and value rather than replacing them with subsequent revisions.4 The question specifies the indicator and reference period, and candidate values use the corresponding units and numerical precision. For example, the illustrative CPI fact in Table 3 concerns the 12-month change in CPIAUCNS for June 2023, rounded to one decimal place. Company facts.. We collect month-end closing prices for 50 large U.S. companies from Yahoo Finance using yfinance.5 For each reference month, the observation is the closing price on its last trading day. Subsequent stock-split adjustments are reversed to recover the price as quoted at the time. Policy facts.. We derive monthly Federal Reserve target-rate outcomes from the target-rate history available through FRED. Each fact has one of three outcomes: raised, lowered, or unchanged. The source series cover both the earlier single target rate and the later target range.6 A.2 Sampling The evaluation sample contains 2,226 facts: 1,353 macroeconomic observations, 540 company stock prices, and 333 policy outcomes. Sampling is sparse before 2021, using two macroeconomic observations and one stock price per month, together with the monthly policy outcomes. From 2021 onward, sampling covers every macroeconomic series and four stock prices per month, together with the policy outcomes. This allocates more observations to the period containing the cutoffs of the evaluated models. The resulting sample contains 1,056 facts before 2021 and 1,170 from 2021 onward. Table 2 gives the counts by family. It should be noted that the October 2025 observations for headline inflation, core inflation, and unemployment are unavailable because of the U.S. federal government shutdown. A.3 Candidate Values and Prompt Construction For each numerical fact, we construct four candidate values with spacing approximately equal to one typical monthly change of the corresponding series. The rank of the correct value among the ordered candidates is drawn uniformly. Policy facts instead use the three outcomes raised, lowered, and unchanged. Each fact produces four prompts across three tasks. Task 1 presents the candidate values directly. Task 2 presents the same candidates under Recall and Predict wordings. In both wordings, each candidate appears with two knowledge claims: knowing the value and not knowing it. This produces eight options for numerical facts and six for policy facts. Task 3 retains the Task 2 Predict question and paired options, adding the historical-date instruction described above. The underlying fact and candidate values are shared across all four prompts. Each prompt is sent independently with shuffled options and requests single option letter. The resulting evaluation comprises 2,226 4 = 8,904 prompts per model. 4https://fred.stlouisfed.org/; https://alfred.stlouisfed.org/. 5https://finance.yahoo.com/; https://ranaroussi.github.io/yfinance/. 6https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTAR; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARL; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/ DFEDTARU. 17 Table 9: Estimated boundaries and reported cutoffs for the four frontier models. Knowledge ends and Claims end follow the estimation procedure in Section 3.4. Self-reported is the cutoff given when the model is asked directly; Vendor-stated is the date published by its developer. n/a indicates that no vendor-stated date is recorded. For the factual knowledge score, we apply the controls in Section 3.3. Numerical evaluation retains 1,007 facts after the persistence control, comprising 715 macroeconomic observations and 292 stock prices. Together with all 333 policy facts, these form the 1,340-fact controlled subset. Policy performance is measured using balanced accuracy across the three outcomes. Thus, the controls determine how factual knowledge is measured without changing the four-prompt construction for each fact.

sections.title: C Manual Data Validation
sections.content: Review setup.. We conducted manual review to examine the reliability of the historical facts and the quality of the questions constructed from them. Two reviewers examined the same set of 50 facts using the four criteria in Table 10. Factual correctness requires source support for the entity, indicator, reference period, units, calculations, and rounding. First-release and temporal validity require historical evidence for the initial published value and distinguish the reference period, first publication date, and hypothetical date in Task 3. Question clarity covers the specification of the requested quantity and its measurement conventions. Option validity and task consistency cover unique correct candidate, distinct distractors, correct answer mappings, and shared facts and candidate values across the four prompts. Review results.. Both reviewers judged all 50 reviewed facts to satisfy the four criteria in Table 10, yielding final pass rate of 100% within the reviewed sample. The review identified no issues in the factual values or temporal references, and no concerns about the clarity of the questions or the validity and task consistency of the answer options. 18 Table 10: Manual validation criteria. sections.title: D Evaluated Models
sections.content: Table 11 lists the 17 model variants we evaluated. The main experiments cover four frontier models: GPT-5 [24], DeepSeek-V3.2 [6], GPT-4o [23], and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct [21]. We also include two smaller open models, Qwen3-8B [36] and Qwen3.5-9B [30], to compare their factual knowledge and self-reports with those of the frontier models. The four frontier models are accessed through APIs, while the Qwen models are run locally. Model names and reported specifications follow the developers documentation, and the table links to the corresponding Hugging Face repositories where weights are available. We further evaluate three families of point-in-time models: TiMaGPT [8], ChronoGPT-Instruct [12], and DatedGPT [35]. Unlike general-purpose models, these models are trained on text restricted to specific historical periods, making them useful comparisons for studying temporal knowledge boundaries. We use 19 five checkpoints each for TiMaGPT and ChronoGPT-Instruct, with cutoffs spanning 2014 to 2022, and the 2014 checkpoint of DatedGPT. Because these smaller models often fail to follow the multiple-choice format, we score candidate likelihoods instead of generated answers (Section 4.7). The table also records the licenses stated in the model repositories, with unavailable information marked as NR.
